evidence: The distinct LC/Wikidata anchor sets describe two authors: a is the Massey medieval historian whose publications include Popular Piety and Civic Ceremony and Religion in Medieval Bruges; b is Andrew Philip Brown (born 1950), the radiation oncologist and biographer of Chadwick, Bernal and Rotblat. These are separate careers, not duplicate authorities.

a combines James Noel Adams's Latin-language scholarship with Aristonikos and the Cistophoroi (1980), which JSTOR credits to John Paul Adams. b is James Noel Adams, author of The Latin Sexual Vocabulary and Bilingualism and the Latin Language. The initials-only key therefore contains more than one author.

a combines Robert Clyde Allen's film/television books with economist Robert Carson Allen's Progress and Poverty in Early Modern Europe. b also combines Attalid history with Robert Edward Allen's dictionaries. LC n80017027 identifies the film scholar; the separate R. E. Allen authority no2014154728 does not establish a shared identity. The work lists are composite.

Cambridge credits King Henry I and Northern England (2007) to Judith Green, matching a's Judith A. anchor. b is the nineteenth-century historian John Richard Green (1837-1883), author of A Short History of the English People. The modern article is not his work or a reprint of it.

a includes Royce L. B. Morris's The Economy of Oxyrhynchus in the First Century alongside R. J. Morris's modern British social-history articles on Samuel Smiles, Scotland and Belfast. b is Richard Morris, the church archaeologist and author of Churches in the Landscape and Guy Gibson. a is a composite initials key, not Richard Morris's bibliography.

a mixes M. G. Smith's Hausa/Jamaican anthropology with other Smiths: the publisher explicitly credits Networks, Territories, and the Cartography of Ancient States (2005) to Monica L. Smith. b's Michael P. Smith has a separate urban-politics and transnationalism bibliography. The M. Smith key cannot represent one person.

a mostly contains education historian Robert D. Anderson's books, but Jewish Persecutions and Weather Shocks (2017) is by Robert Warren Anderson, Johnson and Koyama. b's Nucleus and Nation is by Robert S. Anderson, the India/science scholar. The LC anchors n83039776 and n2004151609 concern distinct careers; a additionally mixes in a third author.

The Collapse of the Gaelic World, 1450-1650 is credited to Steven G. Ellis, matching a's anchor. b is Sylvia Ellis, whose books concern Anglo-American relations, the Vietnam War and Lyndon Johnson. The credited authors and their publication programmes are distinct.

a combines Harlaxton medievalist David Green's Black Prince books with Gentlewomanly Capitalism, which Wiley credits to David R. Green of King's College London and Alastair Owens. b is welfare-policy author David G. Green. LC nb96009926 and n81064409 correspond to the distinct medievalist and policy-author identities; a's works also contain another Green.

The distinct LC authorities n90651658 and n88174101 concern different scholars: a's Elizabeth Harvey is the historian of Weimar/Nazi Germany who wrote Women and the Nazi East; b's Elizabeth D. Harvey is the Renaissance literary scholar and editor of Sensible Flesh, identified by Penn Press with the University of Toronto. Their books establish separate careers.

LC nr93018616 concerns Welsh civil servant Thomas Jones (1870-1955), author of Whitehall Diary; nr90002050 concerns the formerly enslaved North Carolina minister Thomas H. Jones, whose narrative appeared before the Welsh man's birth. a also includes Brut y Tywysogion (1955), edited by another Thomas Jones (1910-1972), as the Dictionary of Welsh Biography confirms.

a combines R. A. Lewis's Chadwick/public-health research with Robert E. Lewis's The English Fabliau Tradition and Chaucer's Miller's Tale (1982), as the publishers credit them. b's Roy Lewis coauthored The English Middle Classes with Angus Maude and wrote books on professions and management. a's abbreviated name pools different authors, not Roy Lewis's career.

a's articles form David Morgan's Mongol-history research, including The Decline and Fall of the Mongol Empire (2009). b is D. H. J. Morgan, the family sociologist whose books include Family Connections and Rethinking Family Practices. Publisher records distinguish the Mongol historian's work from the sociologist's books.

The Cambridge expedition to Vatnajokull was led and described by B. B. Roberts, the polar explorer Brian Birley Roberts; the expedition's contemporary Cambridge account names him. a's Brian K. anchor is therefore misleading. b is Brigham Henry Roberts (1857-1933), the Mormon historian and theologian, whose church histories are a different author's works.

The Journal of Politics credits The Progressive Era in Perspective (1959) to Andrew M. Scott, so a's Allen J. anchor is misleading. b is Alan Scott (born 1956), author of Ideology and the New Social Movements (1990); he was about three when the article appeared. The article and sociology books belong to different people.
